artists.biography: Richard Barbieri has been Porcupine Tree's keyboard/synthesizer player since 1993 (what started as a studio/home project by Steven Wilson developed into a successful touring band with major label releases and a worldwide profile).  Richard's musical career started at the age of 17 when he joined the band Japan. During the early eighties the band achieved commercial and critical success culminating in the groundbreaking album Tin Drum which stayed in the album charts for a year. The album sessions involved Richard in his most intense period of analogue synthesizer programming.  More recently, Richard began to leave the "comfort zone" of his analogue synthesizers in favour of exploring the potential offered by digital synthesizers. His debut solo album Things Buried was released in 2005. He has also been involved in a number of projects with former Japan bandmates David Sylvian, Mick Karn, and Steve Jansen in various combinations, including Rain Tree Crow (which was a full Japan reunion).

perplexity.description:
Hauntings is Richard Barbieri's first studio album since 2021's Under A Spell, released on April 10, 2026 via Kscope. The album deepens the pensive, dark instrumental aesthetic of its predecessor, presenting a diverse collection of immersive sound worlds that blend past and future influences in equal measure. Barbieri's deft keyboard work and sonic architecture conjure a shadowy, creeping Lovecraftian atmosphere, with the music wandering through the streets of a gloomy lamp-lit Victorian London and drifting into grain-speckled snapshots of Belle Époque Paris. The album explores themes of nostalgia for both the past and future, questioning what is real and what is simulation, with the cover's French New Wave design and blood-red logo reflecting this aesthetic vision.

The 11-track album showcases Barbieri at the height of his powers, with influences rooted in the Berlin School of Music tradition exemplified by artists like Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze. Tracks such as "Anemoia" and "Traveler" demonstrate Barbieri's venture into industrial Film-Noir territory, blending late 1940s and early 1950s vibrations with futuristic techno grooves reminiscent of David Bowie's Outside and Radiohead's Kid A sessions. These journeys into the past are contrasted with nihilistic but euphoric forays into the future, with pieces like "Traveler" and "A New Simulation" bristling with the itchy modern anxiety that characterizes his best work.

The album's hypnotic and dreamlike qualities create an immersive sonic experience that paints vivid pictures of two distinct historical worlds. From the opening "Snakes & Ladders" through the contemplative "Last Post," Barbieri constructs intricate sound landscapes that evoke both darkness and uplift, establishing Hauntings as a significant entry in his discography and a testament to his status as one of the most intuitive and unique musicians of his generation.
